name: Kathmandu Valley
tagline: Three Newar cities on an old lake bed
meta_description: Kathmandu Valley with locals: Yen, Yala and Khwopa, stupas, stone spouts, Newar feasts and festivals, best months, stays and trips to Nagarkot and Panauti.
summary: The Kathmandu Valley is a 25 km wide bowl at about 1,400 m holding three old Newar royal cities, Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur, plus seven UNESCO monument zones. Come October to November or March to April, give it four to six days, and walk it tole by tole.
intro: We grew up in this valley, and we still find new courtyards in it. Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur sit within 15 km of each other, yet each kept its own king, its own festivals and its own way of cooking buffalo. In Nepal Bhasa they are Yen, Yala and Khwopa. Between them lie rice terraces, brick villages like Bungamati and Kirtipur, and hilltop shrines such as Changunarayan, where Nepal's oldest dated inscription still stands in the courtyard.

The valley floor sits at about 1,300 to 1,400 m, ringed by forested hills that climb to 2,732 m at Shivapuri. That rim is why the morning views can be so clear in autumn and why smoke and dust settle over the city in late winter. Step up to Nagarkot or Dhulikhel, an hour or so east, and on a clear day the Himalaya fills the northern horizon from Langtang towards Everest.

Most visitors give the valley one rushed day before a trek. We think it deserves four to six. The temples are the obvious draw, but the life around them matters more: women filling copper pots at a hiti, guthi members repairing a rest house, a samay baji plate shared at a family puja, a chariot built by hand every spring in the middle of a Patan road.

The valley is also a place rebuilding. The April 2015 earthquake brought down Kasthamandap, parts of the Durbar Squares and many village houses. Much has been restored with traditional brick, timber and carving, often by local guthis and craftsmen rather than contractors. Walking these squares now, you see old struts beside new ones, and people will happily tell you which is which.

story.title: From lake bed to the cities of the Mallas
paras: Geologists agree with the old stories on one point: the Kathmandu Valley was once a lake. Its soft black clay, the kind that names the Kalimati neighbourhood, is lake sediment, and it is why rice grows so well here and why buildings shake so hard in earthquakes. People settled the drained basin early, and by the Licchavi period, roughly the 5th to 9th centuries CE, kings were carving Sanskrit inscriptions, building water spouts and endowing temples. Changunarayan's pillar of 464 CE and Patan's Manga Hiti date from this time.

From about the 12th century the Malla kings ruled, and in the 15th century the kingdom split among heirs into the rival cities of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur. Competition made them builders. Each king tried to outdo the others with palaces, pagodas, courtyards and stepped tanks, and much of what you see in the three Durbar Squares dates from the 17th and early 18th centuries, under kings such as Pratap Malla, Siddhi Narasimha Malla and Bhupatindra Malla.

In 1768 Prithvi Narayan Shah of Gorkha took Kathmandu during Indra Jatra, after years of blockading the valley and three assaults on Kirtipur. Patan fell the same year and Bhaktapur in 1769. Kathmandu became the capital of a unified Nepal. Under the Rana prime ministers, from 1846 to 1951, white neoclassical palaces rose beside the brick cities, and several, such as the old Rana palaces at Lazimpat and Durbar Marg, are hotels today.

Through all of it, Newar life ran on guthis: trusts that own land and fund a festival, a temple, a cremation, a water spout or a chariot. Many still operate. When the 2015 earthquake struck, it was often guthi members and local craftsmen who sorted the fallen timbers and argued over how each strut should be carved again. The valley you visit is the result of that care, and it is still being repaired.

legend: In the Swayambhu Purana, the valley was a lake called Nagdaha, home to serpent kings. A lotus bloomed on it, giving off a light that was the self-born Buddha, Swayambhu. The bodhisattva Manjushri came from the north, cut a gorge in the southern hills with his sword so the water drained out at Chobhar, and people settled the land. Hindu tellings give the same work to Krishna, who split the hills with his discus. Locals still point to Chobhar gorge as the cut.
people: The Newars are the valley's old townspeople: Buddhist and Hindu, farmers, potters, metalworkers, traders and priests, speaking Nepal Bhasa and organised by caste, clan and guthi. Around them live Tamang communities on the rim hills, Brahmin and Chhetri families who came with the Gorkha state, Tibetans who settled at Boudha and Jawalakhel after 1959, and migrants from every district of Nepal. Nepali is the shared language; Nepal Bhasa is heard most in the old cores.

untold.fact: In 1664 King Pratap Malla set a stone inscription into the wall of the Kathmandu Durbar Square in fifteen languages and scripts. Local tradition says anyone who can read all of them will make milk flow from the spout beneath it.

Nepal Sambat, the Newar lunar calendar, began in 879 CE. Tradition credits a Kathmandu merchant, Sankhadhar Sakhwa, with paying off the people's debts so a new era could start. Newar New Year is still celebrated on the day after Tihar's Laxmi Puja.

The UNESCO World Heritage Site called Kathmandu Valley, inscribed in 1979, is a single listing made up of seven monument zones: the three Durbar Squares, Swayambhu, Boudhanath, Pashupati and Changunarayan. It sat on the List of World Heritage in Danger from 2003 to 2007.

untold.fact: Narayanhiti Palace, the royal palace until the monarchy ended in 2008, takes its name from a stone water spout, the Narayan hiti, at its eastern gate. The palace is now a museum.
The name Kathmandu comes from Kasthamandap, Sanskrit for wooden pavilion: a public rest house in the Durbar Square area that Newars call Maru Satta. The city was also long known as Kantipur.

local_words.meaning: Sunken stone water spout, often Licchavi or Malla era
Community trust that funds a temple, festival or ritual
Neighbourhood or street quarter of an old town
Street festival, often with a chariot or masked dancers

taste.name: Samay baji
taste.text: The Newar ritual plate: beaten rice (baji), smoked buffalo chhoyla, black soybeans, ginger, garlic, fried fish, egg and a splash of aila. It is offered to the gods first and then shared. Try it at a Newar khaja ghar in Patan's Mangal Bazaar or Kirtipur's community-run Newa Lahana.

highlights.title: Three Durbar Squares in three days
highlights.text: Kathmandu's Hanuman Dhoka, Patan's Mangal Bazaar and Bhaktapur's palace square were rival royal seats. Give each its own day. Patan has the finest museum, Bhaktapur the quietest lanes, Kathmandu the living goddess and the busiest markets at Asan and Indra Chowk.

highlights.title: Dawn kora at Boudhanath
highlights.text: Walk clockwise round the great stupa at 6 am with Tibetan grandmothers spinning prayer wheels and monks heading to puja. Climb a rooftop cafe for butter tea as the light reaches the white dome and the eyes on its gilded tower.

highlights.title: Stone spouts that still flow
highlights.text: The valley has hundreds of hitis, sunken stone spouts fed by old channels. Patan's Manga Hiti dates to 570 CE and Kathmandu's Sundhara area takes its name from one. Morning is when neighbours queue with buckets and the carvings are wet.

highlights.title: Newar villages south of the ring road
highlights.text: Bungamati, Khokana and Kirtipur keep brick lanes, open courtyards and craft work. Watch woodcarvers in Bungamati, mustard-oil presses in Khokana and the hilltop temples of Kirtipur, then eat at a cooperative restaurant run by local women.

highlights.title: Himalayan sunrise on the rim
highlights.text: Nagarkot at about 2,175 m and Dhulikhel at about 1,550 m face the high peaks from Langtang eastwards. Stay overnight, set an alarm for 5.30 am in autumn, and walk down next morning through villages to Changunarayan or Namobuddha.

highlights.title: Chariots, masks and a living goddess
highlights.text: Plan around a jatra if you can. Indra Jatra brings out the Kumari's chariot in Kathmandu in September, Bisket Jatra pits Bhaktapur's two halves in a tug of war in April, and Patan pulls Rato Machhindranath's towering chariot in spring.

getting_there: Almost everyone arrives at Tribhuvan International Airport (KTM), about 6 km east of central Kathmandu, with direct flights from Delhi, Mumbai, Doha, Dubai, Istanbul, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Singapore and others. A taxi to Thamel or Patan takes 20 to 45 minutes depending on traffic. Most nationalities can get a visa on arrival (15, 30 or 90 days; fees in USD); Indian citizens need no visa and can enter with a passport or voter ID. Overland from India, the main crossings are Sunauli–Belahiya (about 280 km, 8 to 10 hours to Kathmandu) and Raxaul–Birgunj (about 270 km, 7 to 9 hours). Within the valley, a private car with driver is easiest; local buses and microbuses are cheap but slow. Check current visa and border rules before you travel.
permits: No trekking permit is needed for the valley's towns and temples. Most heritage zones charge foreigners an entry fee at the gate: Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur Durbar Squares, Swayambhu, Boudhanath, Pashupati and Changunarayan all collect one, with lower rates for SAARC nationals and Chinese visitors. Keep your Bhaktapur ticket, as it can be extended with your passport. Hikes on the rim inside Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park need a park entry ticket, and the 2023 rule requiring foreigners to walk with a licensed guide in national parks may apply. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Kathmandu 2–19 °C, dry, cold mornings, hazy afternoons
months.summary: Cold, clear mornings and warm sunny middays. Frost is possible on the rim at Nagarkot, so rooms with heating matter. The month of Magh begins mid-January, and Newar families eat chaku, sesame laddu and sweet potato for Maghe Sankranti. Panauti's riverside ghats fill for Makar Sankranti, and in the twelfth year the town hosts its large Makar mela. Valley haze builds through the afternoons, so do mountain viewpoints early.
months.tip: Pack a down jacket for sunrise at Nagarkot, where dawn sits close to freezing.

months.summary: Days warm up and the tourist crowds are thin. Losar, the Tibetan and Sherpa new year, usually falls in February or March, and Boudhanath fills with families in new chuba, butter lamps and a fresh line of prayer flags. Maha Shivaratri usually falls in February or early March and brings sadhus from across Nepal and India to Pashupatinath. Dust and haze can hide the mountains, so treat views as a bonus.
months.tip: On Shivaratri, reach Pashupatinath before 7 am or expect queues of several hours.

months.summary: One of the best months to walk the cities: long dry days, rhododendrons on the rim hills and comfortable evenings. Holi, the colour festival, falls in March in most years and is lively in Kathmandu's Basantapur. Ghode Jatra, the horse festival at Tundikhel, falls in March or April. Afternoon haze is common, but mornings at Nagarkot and Dhulikhel can still show the peaks.
months.tip: On Holi, wear old clothes and keep phones in zip bags if you plan to walk the old town.

months.summary: Nepali New Year falls in mid-April, and Bhaktapur celebrates it with Bisket Jatra: a week of chariot pulling, a tall pole raised and dropped, and neighbouring Thimi's vermilion-throwing Sindure Jatra. In Patan, Rato Machhindranath's chariot is usually built and begins its weeks-long roll around this time. Warm days, short storms in the late afternoon.
months.tip: Book Bhaktapur rooms early for Bisket week; the old town's small guesthouses fill quickly.

months.summary: The hottest month in the valley, with dust and pre-monsoon thunderstorms. Buddha Jayanti, the Buddha's birthday, usually falls in May, when Swayambhu and Boudha are lit with butter lamps. Rato Machhindranath's chariot is often still moving through Patan, and the Bhoto Jatra at Jawalakhel may fall now or in June. Good month for early starts and long lunches indoors.
months.tip: Walk the stupas at dawn and dusk; middays near 30 °C are tiring on stone squares.

months.summary: The monsoon usually reaches Kathmandu in the second or third week of June. Mornings are often fine, with rain in the afternoon and at night. Paddy planting begins in the fields around Bungamati and Khokana, and the 15th of Asar is Ropain day, when farmers celebrate rice planting with mud and curd and beaten rice. Mountain views are rare.
months.tip: Carry a small umbrella daily and plan museums for wet afternoons.

months.summary: Peak monsoon. Roads to Nagarkot and Dhulikhel can be slowed by landslides and potholes, and the hills are often in cloud. The cities are green and quiet, hotel rates are low, and indoor sights like the Patan Museum and the Narayanhiti Palace Museum come into their own. Leeches appear on rim-hill trails. Trekkers heading for rain-shadow areas pass through.
months.tip: Check road status before any drive out of the valley in July.

months.weather: Kathmandu 20–28 °C, monsoon rain, breaks of sun
months.summary: Still monsoon, but festival season starts. Janai Purnima brings pilgrims to Patan's Kumbheshwar and Gai Jatra follows the next day, when families who lost someone in the past year parade a cow or a child dressed as one through Kathmandu and Bhaktapur. Krishna Janmashtami fills Patan's Krishna Mandir at night. Rain usually comes in bursts.
months.tip: Gai Jatra in Bhaktapur is longer and more theatrical than in Kathmandu; go if you can.

months.weather: Kathmandu 18–27 °C, monsoon easing late in month
months.summary: Indra Jatra takes over Kathmandu's Durbar Square for eight days, with masked dancers, the Kumari's chariot procession and the great mask of Seto Bhairab pouring rice beer. Teej, when women in red fast and dance, brings crowds to Pashupatinath and usually falls in late August or September. Rain thins out towards the end of the month and views start to return.
months.tip: For the Kumari procession, find a stepped temple plinth in Basantapur an hour early.

months.summary: The best month for mountain views and the busiest for visitors. Dashain, Nepal's biggest festival, usually falls in late September or October: families gather, kites fly, swings go up in villages and goats are sacrificed on the eighth and ninth days. Shops and offices close for several days. Nagarkot and Dhulikhel sunrises are at their most reliable.
months.tip: Book transport and hotels well ahead around Dashain, when half the city travels home.

months.summary: Tihar, the festival of lights, usually falls in October or November: oil lamps on every step, garlands for crows, dogs and cows, and Newar Mha Puja and New Year on the same evenings. Days are clear and cool, perfect for long walks like Changunarayan to Bhaktapur or Kirtipur to Chobhar. Evenings are cold enough for a fleece.
months.tip: During Tihar, the old core of Patan and Bhaktapur is lovely after dark, when lamps are lit.

months.summary: Short clear days, cold nights and few visitors. Yomari Punhi, the full moon of December, is when Newar families steam yomari, sweet rice dumplings filled with molasses and sesame, and offer them to the grain stores. Mountain views are still common in the mornings. Valley fog can delay early flights, so plan buffer time before treks.
months.tip: Leave a spare day before domestic mountain flights; morning fog can delay them.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: Four to six days lets you see the three Durbar Squares, Swayambhu, Boudha and Pashupati without rushing, plus one day out to Bungamati, Kirtipur or Changunarayan and a night at Nagarkot or Dhulikhel. With only two days, focus on Patan and Bhaktapur for heritage and Boudhanath for an evening kora, and skip the long drives to the rim.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest skies and the most reliable mountain views, with daytime highs of 23 to 26 °C. March and April are the second-best window, warmer and hazier, with Bisket Jatra in April. December and January are cold but clear and quiet. June to August is monsoon: cities are fine, views rare.

faqs.q: Is the Kathmandu Valley safe for tourists?
faqs.a: Yes, for most travellers it is. Petty theft and taxi overcharging are the usual problems. Protests and general strikes do happen, sometimes at short notice, and can close roads for a day; follow local news and your hotel's advice. Traffic is the larger daily risk, so take care crossing ring-road junctions. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which is better, Patan or Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Both, if you can. Patan is closer to central Kathmandu, has the best museum in Nepal inside its palace and a dense web of Buddhist courtyards. Bhaktapur is quieter and more complete as a town, with fewer cars in its core, potters working in the open and tall temples like Nyatapola. If you must pick one for an overnight stay, pick Bhaktapur.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide in Kathmandu?
faqs.a: No permit requires one in the cities, but a good local guide changes the experience: they read the inscriptions, explain which god sits in which shrine, and take you through courtyards you would walk past. We suggest a guide for the first Durbar Square day and for Pashupatinath, then exploring on your own. Licensed guides are needed for national-park hikes.

faqs.q: How much are the entry fees to heritage sites?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay at each site. Kathmandu and Patan Durbar Squares have charged about NPR 1,000, Bhaktapur around NPR 1,500 to 1,800, Pashupatinath about NPR 1,000, and Swayambhu and Boudha a few hundred rupees each. SAARC nationals pay much less. Fees change often, so check current status before you travel and carry cash in rupees.

faqs.q: Can I see the Himalaya from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Sometimes, from rooftops on clear autumn and winter mornings, but the best views are from the rim. Nagarkot (about 2,175 m) and Dhulikhel (about 1,550 m) face the range from Langtang eastwards, and Everest can appear as a small peak on very clear days. Go October to February and be up by 6 am.

faqs.q: What should I eat in the Kathmandu Valley?
faqs.a: Eat Newar food at least twice. Order samay baji, chhoyla, bara (lentil patties), chatamari, kachila and juju dhau, the thick sweet curd of Bhaktapur. Momos are everywhere and best from small local shops. For a full sit-down Newar meal, Patan and Kirtipur have good family-run places; for Tibetan food, go to Boudha.

faqs.q: Is the valley still damaged from the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Mostly rebuilt. Kasthamandap, the Boudhanath dome, Patan's temples and many of Bhaktapur's monuments have been restored, and Kathmandu's Hanuman Dhoka palace has been under long restoration. You will still see scaffolding, props and some empty plinths in villages such as Bungamati. Visiting helps: entry fees fund heritage repair and local guides.
